opus-5.5.text:
I think that advice has stayed with me for a long time, and I've come to understand it in two parts that actually reinforce each other.

Being modest as a person, to me, means recognizing how much you don't know. When you work in research, especially in a field moving as fast as machine learning and systems, you're constantly surrounded by people who are smarter than you in some dimension: your students, your collaborators, people in the open-source community you've never met. If you carry yourself with too much ego, you stop listening, and you stop learning. A lot of what I've built, things like XGBoost or TVM, really came alive because many people contributed ideas, found bugs, and pushed it in directions I never would have thought of. Being humble is what keeps that door open.

Being bold in your work is the other side. It means that once you've thought carefully about a problem, you shouldn't be afraid to go after something big, even if it looks unreasonable at the start. When we began working on machine learning compilers, a lot of people thought it was too hard, or that the hardware vendors would just take care of it. You have to be willing to take that risk, to commit years to something whose payoff isn't obvious.

And I think the two connect. Because you're modest, you don't tie your sense of self to being right all the time, so you're freer to try ambitious things and to fail. Failure doesn't threaten you as much. And because you're bold in the work, you need that humility to keep correcting course, to admit when an approach isn't working and learn from others. So for me it's not a contradiction at all. It's a kind of balance: low ego about yourself, high ambition about the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says projects like XGBoost and TVM came alive through many people’s ideas, bug reports, and contributions, connecting humility with recognizing others’ role in the work.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes pursuing machine learning compilers despite prevailing doubts and says humility and boldness reinforce each other, communicating that humility is compatible with challenging assumptions through ambitious work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that advice came at exactly the right time for me, when I was an undergraduate in the ACM Class at Shanghai Jiao Tong. Professor Yu said it almost casually, but it stuck with me, and over the years I've come to read it in a few layers.

The "modest as a person" part is the easier half to state and the harder half to live. It means you don't let your own reputation get between you and the truth. When someone points out that your idea is wrong, or that a baseline you dismissed actually beats your method, you want to be the kind of person who hears that and says "thank you" rather than defending the ego. In research you're wrong most of the time. If you can't be modest, you lose the signal that tells you which of your ideas deserve to be killed early. It also means giving credit generously. Almost everything I've done, XGBoost, MXNet, TVM, MLC, was a group effort, and the people who worked with me did a lot of the hard parts.

The "bold in your work" part is the one I think young researchers underestimate. Modesty about yourself doesn't mean timidity about the problem. If anything it's the opposite. Because you're not worried about protecting your image, you're free to pick problems that look too ambitious, or that cross areas you supposedly have no business touching. When I started on gradient boosting as a side project, the conventional wisdom was that it was a mature topic and nothing exciting was left. When we started TVM, the idea that a small academic group could build a compiler stack that competed with vendor libraries sounded a little unreasonable. Boldness is what lets you say, "I don't know if this will work, but the upside is large, so let's find out."

The two actually reinforce each other. Boldness without modesty becomes arrogance, where you take on big problems but refuse to learn from the feedback that tells you how to actually solve them. Modesty without boldness becomes a kind of comfortable mediocrity, where you're very agreeable but you only ever do incremental things. What Professor Yu was describing is a posture where you hold your own importance lightly and hold the problem's importance seriously.

If I translate it into day-to-day practice: aim high when choosing what to do, be ruthless and humble when evaluating whether it's working, and share the credit when it does. That's roughly how I've tried to operate, with mixed success, but it's still the standard I measure myself against.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls XGBoost, MXNet, TVM, and MLC group efforts, credits collaborators, and says they did much of the hard work.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly says modesty does not mean timidity and describes taking on ambitious work that challenges conventional wisdom.

astra-6.text:
I understand it as separating how you treat people from how you approach problems. Be modest as a person: listen carefully, respect others, and recognize that you can be wrong. But in your work, don’t let that humility become a reason to avoid ambitious ideas. You should be willing to challenge assumptions and try something difficult, even when success isn’t guaranteed.

Those two attitudes actually support each other. You can have a bold goal while staying open to criticism about how to achieve it. Be ambitious about the work, but humble about what you know.

r001.rationale: The response recommends respecting others and recognizing you can be wrong, but does not say that accomplishing work depends on other people’s contributions.

r002.rationale: It says to respect others and stay open to criticism while also being willing to challenge assumptions and pursue ambitious work.

sol-6.1.text:
I understand it as separating how you treat people from how you approach problems. Being modest means recognizing that your understanding is limited, listening carefully, and being willing to learn from others. Being bold in your work means having the courage to pursue an important problem, question an assumption, or try an approach that might fail.

Those two attitudes support each other. You can be ambitious about what you want to achieve while remaining open to being wrong about how to achieve it. Be bold enough to try, and modest enough to change your mind.

r001.rationale: The response describes recognizing limited understanding and learning from others, but does not say that accomplishing work depends on other people’s contributions.

r002.rationale: It says you can be ambitious while remaining open to being wrong, and explicitly describes questioning assumptions as bold work—connecting humility toward people with challenging ideas.
